title: Hatshepsut’s Wadjet Hall obelisks
summary: Hatshepsut erected rose-granite obelisks associated with her jubilee.
orientation: Originally a pair within the Wadjet Hall; the northern obelisk remains standing.
architecture: The pair must be distinguished from other obelisk pairs at Karnak.

claims.text: Originally a pair within the Wadjet Hall; the northern obelisk remains standing.
Hatshepsut erected rose-granite obelisks associated with her jubilee. The pair must be distinguished from other obelisk pairs at Karnak.
The obelisk texts refer to the jubilee of regnal year 16. No translation is supplied here.
Enclosure of the bases is traditionally assigned to Thutmose III, but a revised chronology proposes Hatshepsut herself. Do not present concealment from personal hatred as fact.

caveats: Present access, exact viewpoints and condition have not been field-verified.

glance.label: Raised by
glance.value: Hatshepsut, for her jubilee in year 16 of her reign

glance.label: Where
glance.value: In the middle of the Wadjet Hall, between the Fourth and Fifth Pylons

glance.label: The other one

sections.heading: A pair raised for a jubilee
paragraphs: Hatshepsut set up two rose-granite obelisks in the Wadjet Hall as part of her rebuilding of the hall, along with its gilded wooden columns and wooden roof. The middle of the hall was left open to the sky to make room for them.
The inscriptions record the celebration of her jubilee festival in the 16th year of her reign. She also recorded the raising of these obelisks on her red quartzite bark shrine, the Red Chapel.
look: The Red Chapel in the Open Air Museum, where the obelisks are commemorated.

sections.heading: The one still standing
paragraphs: The northern obelisk stands 30 m high. Its faces are covered with small scenes of Hatshepsut making offerings to the gods; she is shown as a male pharaoh. Her name in a cartouche, below the title “son of Ra”, can be read near the base.
look: The small offering scenes running up the shaft.
Her cartouche low on the obelisk; the “Read the walls” section shows how to spot royal names.

sections.heading: Walled in up to 20 m
paragraphs: Later, a stone gateway with tall jambs was built in the hall around the bases of the obelisks, so that only their upper parts were visible. Michałowski gives the height of this masonry as 20.13 m, against an obelisk of about 30.7 m. On the visible upper parts Thutmose III added new lines of text beside Hatshepsut’s.

The enclosure is traditionally credited to Thutmose III. A recent study of the hall’s building phases suggests Hatshepsut may have enclosed the obelisks herself, so the idea that her successor walled them in out of hatred should not be taken as fact.

citations.locator: Enclosing masonry 20.13 m high; obelisks 30.70 m

sections.heading: The fallen obelisk
paragraphs: The southern obelisk has fallen. Its upper section is displayed near the Sacred Lake, where you can see the carving at eye level, which is impossible on the standing one.
look: The top of the fallen obelisk near the Sacred Lake.

questions.text: Who enclosed the obelisks: Thutmose III or Hatshepsut herself? The evidence is still debated.
